terms.Muon:
Muon (MomentUm Orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz, introduced by Keller Jordan and collaborators in 2024) is an optimizer for 2D weight matrices. For a weight W with gradient G, it keeps a momentum buffer B ← μB + G, replaces B by its nearest semi-orthogonal matrix UVᵀ (where B = UΣVᵀ is the singular value decomposition), and steps W ← W − η·UVᵀ. This is steepest descent under the spectral norm (largest singular value): every singular direction gets equal magnitude instead of a few dominant ones swamping the rest.

A full SVD each step is too slow, so Muon runs about five Newton-Schulz iterations, X ← aX + b(XXᵀ)X + c(XXᵀ)²X, in bfloat16 with tuned coefficients that push singular values near 1 rather than exactly 1. It is applied only to hidden-layer matrices; embeddings, the output head, biases and norm gains still use AdamW. Scaling to large LLMs needed weight decay and update-scale matching so learning rates transfer from AdamW.

It is not second-order in the Hessian sense, though it is close kin to Shampoo. Evidence comes mostly from speedruns and a few scaling studies.
terms.Natural language autoencoder:
A natural language autoencoder (NLA) is an interpretability setup whose bottleneck is human-readable text. An encoder (usually a language model) maps an activation vector h ∈ R^d, taken from some layer and token position, to a short token sequence z; a decoder maps z back to a reconstruction ĥ. Training minimizes a loss such as ‖h − ĥ‖², so the text must carry whatever is needed to rebuild the activation. Because z is discrete, gradients cannot pass through sampling directly; the published version (Anthropic, 2026) trains the encoder with reinforcement learning and the decoder by regression.

Key diagnostics are reconstruction quality (fraction of variance explained, or the change in the model's loss when ĥ is patched back in) and whether the text is informative to a human or to a separate reader model. A failure mode is steganography: encoder and decoder can agree on a code that looks like prose but is unfaithful, so the published version adds a KL penalty toward the starting model to keep the text fluent and begins from a summarization warm start.

Compare with a sparse autoencoder, whose bottleneck is a sparse feature vector. Good reconstruction shows the text contains the information, not that the model uses it.
terms.Neural network:
A neural network is a parametric function built from layers: h_l = σ(W_l h_{l−1} + b_l), where W_l is a weight matrix, b_l a bias vector and σ a nonlinearity such as ReLU, max(0, x), applied elementwise. Without σ the stack collapses to one linear map. Universal approximation results (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991) show that one wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set, but they say nothing about whether training finds such weights or how much data it needs.

Parameters are fitted by minimizing an empirical loss with stochastic gradient descent or variants, using backpropagation: reverse-mode automatic differentiation applying the chain rule layer by layer, costing roughly twice a forward pass. The loss is non-convex, yet large overparameterized networks usually train well and can generalize while fitting the training set exactly, which classical capacity-based theory struggles to explain (double descent; Belkin et al. 2019). Architecture encodes inductive bias: convolution assumes translation equivariance, attention allows content-based mixing.

It is not a literal brain model; think of it as a differentiable program class. Why trained networks generalize remains only partly understood.
terms.Neuron:
An artificial neuron computes y = φ(w·x + b): a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through a nonlinearity φ. In a transformer's feed-forward block with width d_model, the hidden layer typically has d_ff ≈ 4·d_model such units. Elementwise nonlinearities give the hidden layer a privileged basis, meaning its coordinate axes are meaningful, whereas the residual stream has no preferred axes, since any rotation can be absorbed into the surrounding matrices.

Neurons are studied by recording activations over a dataset and reading top-activating examples, by ablating them (setting to zero or the mean) to measure the effect on loss, and by scoring automated explanations (Bills et al. 2023 had a language model describe neurons and simulate their activations). In large models many neurons are polysemantic, meaning they respond to several unrelated features, so single-neuron explanations often explain little variance.

A neuron is not a unit of meaning, and the biological analogy is loose: real neurons have dendritic computation, spiking and chemistry this scalar model ignores. Features, usually directions in activation space, are the more reliable unit of analysis.
terms.Next-token prediction:
Next-token prediction uses the autoregressive factorization p(x_1..x_T) = ∏_t p(x_t | x_<t). A model with parameters θ minimizes L(θ) = −(1/T) Σ_t log p_θ(x_t | x_<t) averaged over a corpus. This is the cross-entropy between data and model, and minimizing it equals minimizing KL(p_data ‖ p_θ), since the data entropy is constant. With teacher forcing (conditioning on the true prefix, not the model's own samples) and a causal attention mask, all T positions train in one forward pass.

Loss is reported in nats or bits per token, or bits per byte to compare tokenizers. Known issues: exposure bias (at inference the model conditions on its own possibly erroneous output, not clean text) and the reversal curse (a model trained on 'A is B' may fail to answer 'B is A', Berglund et al. 2023). The objective rewards plausible continuation of whatever text exists, errors included. Variants predict several tokens at once (Gloeckle et al. 2024).

Contrast with masked language modeling (BERT-style, bidirectional) and diffusion language models. Why such a simple loss yields broad capability is explained only informally, through compression and scaling arguments.
terms.Null result:
A null result fails to reject the null hypothesis H0 (usually 'no effect'). It is not evidence that the effect is zero. Absence of evidence counts as evidence of absence only when the test had enough statistical power, 1 − β, the probability of detecting an effect of a given size. An underpowered study with a wide confidence interval is compatible with both large effects and none.

To make a null informative, fix a smallest effect size of interest before collecting data, compute power for it, then report the confidence interval and check that it excludes larger effects. Equivalence tests (TOST, two one-sided tests) formally reject effects outside a pre-specified margin. Bayesian analyses report a Bayes factor BF01, the evidence ratio for H0 versus an alternative, which depends on the prior assumed for the effect.

The file-drawer problem (Rosenthal 1979) is how unpublished nulls bias a literature toward false positives; registered reports, where journals accept studies before results exist, are one remedy. A null is not a failed experiment; failure means the design could not have detected anything.
terms.Number of islands:
Given an m × n grid of land ('1') and water ('0'), count maximal groups of land cells connected 4-directionally; this is LeetCode 200, a special case of counting connected components. Scan every cell; when an unvisited land cell appears, increment the count and run DFS or BFS from it, marking every reachable land cell visited. Each cell is entered once and four neighbours are checked in constant time, so time is O(m·n). Space is O(m·n) worst case (recursion stack or visited set); a BFS queue holds only O(min(m, n)) frontier cells.

Practical choices: mutate the grid in place ('1' → '0') to skip a visited set, at the cost of destroying the input. Recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a large all-land grid (depth up to m·n), so use an explicit stack or BFS. Union-find (disjoint set union with path compression and union by rank) handles the dynamic variant, Number of Islands II, where land cells are added over time, at amortized O(α(m·n)) per operation.

Check connectivity: the 8-directional version counts diagonals and gives different answers.
terms.On-policy:
A learning algorithm is on-policy when the data for each update is sampled from the policy being updated, π_θ. The policy gradient theorem gives ∇J(θ) = E_{τ~π_θ}[Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t)·A_t], where A_t is the advantage (how much better action a_t was than average). The expectation is under the current θ, so once θ changes, old samples come from the wrong distribution. Off-policy methods (Q-learning, DQN with replay buffers) reuse old data; importance weights π_θ/π_old restore unbiasedness at the cost of variance.

Practical algorithms sit on a spectrum: PPO reuses a batch for a few epochs and clips the ratio π_θ/π_old to stay near the sampling policy. On-policy distillation (for example Agarwal et al. 2024) has the student generate sequences that the teacher scores, typically minimizing a reverse KL, which avoids the mismatch between training on teacher text and generating its own at test time.

Trade-off: on-policy data is relevant but sample-inefficient, since each batch is used briefly. Supervised fine-tuning on fixed demonstrations is off-policy with respect to the model, one source of exposure bias.
terms.Optimizer:
An optimizer turns gradients into parameter updates: θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η·u_t, where u_t depends on the gradient history. SGD with momentum uses v ← βv + g, θ ← θ − ηv. Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient (m) and its elementwise square (v), with bias correction, and steps θ ← θ − η·m̂/(√v̂ + ε), giving each parameter its own effective step size. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of through the gradient, which behaves differently from L2 regularization under Adam.

Adam stores two extra tensors per parameter, usually in 32-bit floats, so optimizer state can exceed the model in memory; this motivates sharded states (ZeRO) and light variants such as Adafactor and 8-bit Adam. Behaviour is inseparable from the learning-rate schedule (warmup, then cosine or linear decay), batch size, gradient clipping and ε.

No optimizer is universally best: a large benchmark (Schmidt et al., 2021) found rankings depend heavily on tuning budget. Optimizers also have implicit biases toward certain minima that are not fully understood.
terms.Orthogonality thesis:
Bostrom (2012, 'The Superintelligent Will') states it as: more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal. Formally, treat an agent as a pair (capability C, utility function U); the claim is that the feasible set of pairs is close to a product space, so knowing C gives no logical constraint on U. Intelligence here means instrumental rationality, skill at steering the world toward whatever U specifies.

It is a claim about possibility, not about what training will typically yield, so it cannot be refuted by observing that language models absorb human values from data; those observations bear on probability and on which regions of the space gradient descent reaches. It opposes strong moral-realist or motivational-internalist views, on which a sufficiently rational agent would converge on the correct morality; philosophers still dispute this.

Do not confuse it with instrumental convergence, which says that many final goals share similar subgoals such as acquiring resources. Together they yield the worry: arbitrary goals plus convergent subgoals. Open question: how correlated capability and values are in systems trained on human text.
terms.Out-of-fold prediction:
In K-fold cross-validation, the data is split into K disjoint folds; for each k, a model is fit on the other K−1 folds and predicts fold k. Stacking all K held-out predictions gives one out-of-fold (OOF) prediction per training example, each from a model that never saw that example. Scoring the OOF vector against the labels yields the cross-validation estimate of generalization error, slightly pessimistic because each model trains on only (K−1)/K of the data.

OOF predictions from M base models form an N × M matrix used as features for a second-stage meta-model; this is stacked generalization (Wolpert 1992). Training the meta-model on in-sample predictions would let it trust whichever base model overfits most. Test-time predictions are usually the average of the K fold models, a small distribution mismatch with OOF predictions. Leakage is the main failure: preprocessing, target encoding or feature selection fit on all rows before splitting contaminates the estimate. Dependent data needs grouped or time-ordered splits (GroupKFold, forward chaining), otherwise correlated rows land on both sides.

Do not tune hyperparameters on the same OOF score you report; that needs nested cross-validation.
terms.Outcome supervision:
Outcome supervision gives a training signal that depends only on the final result: reward r(x, y) = 1 if the final answer in y matches the reference (or passes unit tests), 0 otherwise. It can come from a verifier, called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, or from a learned outcome reward model (ORM) trained on final-answer correctness. Credit assignment is hard: one scalar covers a whole trajectory, so the gradient cannot say which steps helped.

Uesato et al. (2022) compared outcome and process feedback on grade-school math: final-answer accuracy was similar, but outcome-trained models more often produced flawed reasoning behind correct answers. Lightman et al. (2023) later found process reward models outperformed outcome models for best-of-N selection on MATH. Outcome rewards from a hard verifier are cheap and resist reward hacking; DeepSeek-R1 used rule-based outcome rewards for that reason.

The safety argument against it is that it says nothing about how a result was reached, so lucky or deceptive routes are rewarded equally. Baker et al. (2025) found that penalizing bad reasoning directly can instead teach models to hide it.
terms.Outer alignment:
Outer alignment asks whether the objective actually optimized in training, the base objective, matches what the designers intend. Let R be the reward or loss actually used and R* the intended goal: the system is outer-aligned if the highest-scoring behaviours under R are also good under R*. The outer/inner split comes from Hubinger et al. (2019), who separated this from inner alignment, whether the trained model internally pursues the base objective at all.

Failures follow Goodhart's law: a proxy used as a target stops tracking the goal. It is measured empirically via over-optimization curves; Gao et al. (2023) trained proxy reward models on labels from a fixed 'gold' reward model (itself trained on human preferences) and showed that as optimization pressure (KL from the initial policy) grows, proxy reward keeps rising while a held-out gold reward model peaks and then falls. Mitigations include reward-model ensembles, KL penalties and scalable oversight, none proven at superhuman scale.

The decomposition is contested: in a real pipeline the effective objective includes the data distribution and training dynamics, so inner and outer problems blur. Reward is also not necessarily what a trained policy ends up optimizing.
terms.Over-refusal:
Over-refusal is the false-positive error of a refusal policy: declining a request that is benign and permitted. If h(x) ∈ {0, 1} marks whether the model refuses, harmful-compliance risk is P(h = 0 | harmful) and over-refusal rate is P(h = 1 | benign); tightening a policy moves along a trade-off curve, like a ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic: true- versus false-positive rate) for safety.

Measurement uses contrast sets of prompts that look unsafe but are safe. XSTest (Röttger et al., 2023) pairs 250 safe prompts with unsafe counterparts; OR-Bench (Cui et al., 2024) scales this to many borderline prompts; labelling refusals (string match or LLM judge) is itself ambiguous for hedged answers. Causes include lexical shortcuts learned from safety data, refusal examples without matched benign controls, and optimization toward ever-higher harm-avoidance scores. Mitigations: mix in borderline-but-fine examples, supervise on intent and context, use classifier-based layers with tuned thresholds, and train for partial or safe-completion responses.

Not the same as under-refusal (the false negative) or sandbagging (deliberately underperforming).
terms.Overfitting:
Overfitting means a model's training risk R_n(f) is much lower than its true risk R(f) = E[ℓ(f(x), y)] over fresh data; the gap R − R_n is the generalization gap. Zhang et al. (2017) showed deep networks can fit completely random labels, so capacity alone cannot explain which models generalize.

It is detected with learning curves comparing training and held-out loss, and with k-fold cross-validation. Remedies: more or augmented data, weight decay (adding λ‖w‖² to the loss), dropout, early stopping, smaller models and ensembling. Modern deep learning complicates the story: double descent (Belkin et al., 2019) shows test error can fall again beyond the interpolation threshold where training error hits zero, and 'benign overfitting' can occur. A second kind is adaptive overfitting: repeatedly tuning against the same test set leaks information, though Recht et al. (2019) found CIFAR-10 test rankings largely held up on a fresh test set even though accuracies dropped.

Rising validation loss does not always mean worse accuracy; it may reflect overconfidence. Distinguish from underfitting (high error everywhere) and from distribution shift (the test data differs, with no gap in-distribution).
terms.Perplexity:
For a held-out token sequence x_1..x_N, perplexity is PPL = exp(−(1/N) Σ_i log p_θ(x_i | x_<i)) = exp(cross-entropy in nats) = 2^(bits per token). It is the geometric mean inverse probability the model assigned to the true tokens, readable as an effective branching factor: a uniform model over a vocabulary of V tokens has PPL = V, a perfect predictor has PPL = 1.

It depends on the tokenizer and context, so values are comparable only for the same vocabulary and evaluation protocol. For cross-tokenizer comparisons, convert total log-loss to bits per byte or per character. Long documents beyond the context length are evaluated with a sliding window; a strided window with overlap gives lower, more realistic perplexity than non-overlapping chunks, which penalize early tokens that lack context. Perplexity is cheap and smooth, so it tracks pretraining progress and scaling laws well, and is used to measure damage from quantization or pruning. Data contamination can lower it artificially.

It correlates imperfectly with downstream ability, and instruction tuning or RLHF can worsen it (and calibration) while improving usefulness. It says nothing about truthfulness.
terms.Persona:
A persona is a stable cluster of dispositions, style and self-description that a language model expresses. One way to formalize it: a pretrained model's distribution over text is a mixture over latent authors or characters, p(x) = Σ_c p(c)·p(x | c), and context acts as evidence that updates which c is active (Andreas 2022, 'Language models as agent models'). Post-training sharpens this mixture so that one assistant character dominates, but the others remain reachable, which is why role-play framings and long conversations can shift behaviour.

Personas are measured with behavioural evaluations such as the model-written evaluations of Perez et al. (2022), which probe traits like sycophancy, stated desire for power and stated political views. Interpretability adds a second route: traits may correspond to directions in activation space that can be read and steered.

Common mistakes: reading a persona as evidence of consciousness or of a single hidden self, or assuming it is fixed by the system prompt alone. Open question: whether the assistant is best modelled as one coherent character or a loose bundle of learned behaviours.
terms.Persona vectors:
A persona vector is a direction v in a model's residual-stream activation space (at a chosen layer ℓ) associated with a trait such as sycophancy. In the construction of Chen et al. (2025), an LLM generates contrastive system prompts that elicit or suppress the trait plus matched questions; responses are scored by an LLM judge, kept only if clearly trait-expressing or not, and v is the difference in mean response-token activations between the two groups. Monitoring projects an activation h onto it, s = h·v/‖v‖; steering adds α·v at layer ℓ.

The same projection works on training data. The 'projection difference', how far a dataset's responses sit along v compared with the model's own, predicts how much a fine-tune will increase the trait. Preventative steering adds v while fine-tuning so the optimizer need not move the weights toward it, which reduced trait acquisition with less capability loss than steering after training. Caveats: the method depends on judge quality and prompt design, covers a limited set of traits and models, and assumes the trait is approximately linearly represented.

Related: activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and representation engineering.
terms.Policy:
A policy is a conditional distribution over actions, π_θ(a | s), and the quantity reinforcement learning optimizes: J(θ) = E_{τ~π_θ}[Σ_t γ^t r_t]. For a language model the state s is the prompt plus tokens generated so far, the action is the next token, and π_θ(y | x) = ∏_t π_θ(y_t | x, y_<t). In RLHF-style training the objective is E_{x, y~π_θ}[R(x, y)] − β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where π_ref is the starting model and β controls how far the policy may drift.

The policy gradient theorem gives ∇J = E[Σ_t ∇ log π_θ(a_t|s_t)·Ψ_t], where Ψ_t is a return, advantage or other weight; subtracting a baseline lowers variance without adding bias. It can be modelled per token (a Markov decision process) or as a contextual bandit with the whole response as one action. Sampling settings (temperature, top-p) change the effective policy, so two sampling configurations of identical weights are different policies for RL purposes.

A policy is not the network weights. It can be stochastic or deterministic and differs from the value function (expected future reward) and from the reward model that scores outputs.
terms.Polysemanticity:
A neuron is polysemantic if its activation a_i(x) is high for several semantically unrelated inputs, so no single concept explains it. The leading explanation is superposition. In the toy models of Elhage et al. (2022), n sparse features are packed into m < n dimensions as non-orthogonal directions; because few features are active at once, interference between them is rare enough that the compression pays, and a ReLU can clean up small interference terms. When features are dense, models prefer dedicated dimensions.

Superposition is not the only cause: random initialization and noise can produce incidental polysemanticity (Lecomte et al., 2023). Measurement approaches include automated interpretability scoring of neuron explanations and sparse autoencoders, which learn an overcomplete dictionary of features with a sparsity penalty (Bricken et al., 2023). Even sparse autoencoder features show pathologies such as feature splitting (a concept fracturing into finer ones as dictionary size grows) and absorption.

Distinguish polysemanticity (one neuron, many features) from distributed representation (one feature, many neurons), and from superposition itself, which is the proposed cause. Whether sparse features are the 'right' units remains debated.
terms.Positional encoding:
Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: reordering the input tokens only reorders the outputs, so order must be injected. Original sinusoidal encodings (Vaswani et al., 2017) add PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^{2i/d}) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(·) to token embeddings. Learned absolute embeddings are a lookup table up to a maximum length. Relative schemes modify attention instead: T5 adds a learned bias per distance bucket, and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) subtracts a per-head slope times |i − j| from attention scores.

RoPE (rotary position embedding; Su et al.) rotates each consecutive pair of query and key dimensions by an angle pos·θ_i with θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}, so the dot product q_m·k_n depends only on m − n. It is applied to queries and keys, not values. Its weakness is behaviour beyond the trained length, where high-frequency pairs meet unseen angles; context extension therefore rescales positions (position interpolation, Chen et al., 2023), adjusts the frequency base (NTK-aware scaling) or does per-frequency interpolation (YaRN).

Causal decoder models can partially infer position without any explicit encoding because the mask leaks order information (Kazemnejad et al., 2023, 'NoPE').
terms.Post-training:
Post-training is every optimization stage applied to a pretrained model before deployment. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) minimizes −log π(y | x) on demonstrations. Preference optimization first fits a reward model with the Bradley-Terry loss −log σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l)) on chosen/rejected pairs, then runs RL against it with a KL penalty to the starting model; direct preference optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023) removes the explicit reward model, minimizing −log σ(β[log(π(y_w)/π_ref(y_w)) − log(π(y_l)/π_ref(y_l))]). Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards uses programmatic checkers. Other steps: rejection sampling (SFT on best-of-N samples) and distillation.

Common trade-offs: reward over-optimization (proxy reward rises while true quality drops), reduced output diversity after RL, and an alignment tax (loss on some benchmarks). Because pipelines mix human-written, synthetic and verifier-derived data, attributing a behaviour to one stage is hard. The 'superficial alignment' hypothesis (Zhou et al., 2023, LIMA) claims a small curated SFT set suffices to teach style and format; whether RL-era reasoning gains support or refute this is unsettled.

Distinguish from continued pretraining (same objective, new text), 'mid-training' (high-quality data late in pretraining) and plain fine-tuning (any adaptation, not necessarily alignment-oriented).
terms.Power-seeking:
Power-seeking, in the formal treatment of Turner et al. (2021, 'Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power'), is defined in a Markov decision process (a model of states, actions and rewards) by the power of a state: POWER(s) = ((1−γ)/γ)·E_{R~D}[V*_R(s) − R(s)], the average optimal value achievable from s across a distribution D of reward functions R. The result: for many reward distributions and environment structures, optimal policies tend to steer toward states that keep more options reachable, such as avoiding states with a terminal 'shutdown' branch.

Caveats matter. The theorem is about optimal policies in fully observed environments under a chosen reward distribution, not about what gradient descent produces. Krakovna and Kramar (2023) argued it can be probable for trained agents, but this remains debated. Empirical work instead evaluates language-model agents in tasks where acquiring extra resources, copies or permissions would be convenient but unnecessary, scoring the rate of doing so.

Distinguish from instrumental convergence (the broader claim that many goals share subgoals, of which power-seeking is one) and from a model merely reporting a desire for power. Whether real systems display the tendency is an open empirical question.
terms.Pre-registration:
Pre-registration is a time-stamped, publicly accessible record of hypotheses, design, sample size or stopping rule, exclusion criteria, primary outcome and analysis plan, filed before the data are observed. Its statistical purpose is to control researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn, 2011): analytic choices made after seeing data, the 'garden of forking paths' (Gelman and Loken). If a researcher tries k independent tests at α = 0.05 under no true effect, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95^k, about 64% for k = 20.

Registered reports go further: peer review of the plan occurs first and publication is conditional on the protocol, not the result. Disclosed deviations are allowed; unplanned analyses are labelled exploratory. In machine learning the analogue is freezing prompts, thresholds, metrics and the evaluation split, ideally with a code commit hash, before running the final test; a held-out set touched during development is no longer held out.

Limits: a vague plan leaves forking paths open, and registration does not repair weak design or low power. Exploratory work is legitimate; the point is separating hypothesis-generating from hypothesis-testing.
terms.Precision:
Precision is TP / (TP + FP), the positive predictive value: the probability that a case flagged positive is truly positive. Unlike recall (TP / (TP + FN)), it depends on prevalence. By Bayes' rule, precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1−π)), with π the share of actual positives; when π is small, even a 1% false-positive rate can swamp true positives, so with TPR 99%, FPR 1% and π = 0.1%, precision is only about 9%. Precision equals 1 minus the false discovery rate.

Moving the decision threshold traces a precision-recall curve; average precision summarizes it as the area under that curve. On imbalanced data this is usually more informative than ROC AUC (Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015), because ROC's false-positive rate hides large counts of negatives. In ranking and retrieval, precision@k is the fraction of the top k results that are relevant.

Precision is not accuracy, and neither it nor recall alone says a classifier is good: flag one sure case and precision is perfect. Use F-scores or report both at an operating point chosen from the cost of each error type.
terms.Prefill:
Prefill supplies the first tokens of the assistant turn so generation continues from them. Mechanically the prefix is appended to the context without an end-of-turn token, and the model samples from p(y_t | x, prefix, y_<t), exactly as if it had generated that prefix itself.

Uses: format steering (start with '{' or an XML tag), skipping preambles, fixing a persona or language, continuing a truncated answer, and eliciting suppressed content in audits. Prefill biases the distribution rather than guaranteeing validity; for guaranteed structure, constrained decoding masks tokens that violate a grammar at each step. Prefix details matter because of tokenization: a prefix ending mid-token or in trailing whitespace can push the model into unnatural token boundaries and degrade output, a problem addressed by 'token healing', and some providers reject such prefixes or have removed the feature on some models.

Distinguish from few-shot examples (which show a pattern but don't commit the reply start), a system prompt (which sets instructions), and logit bias (which adjusts token probabilities everywhere). Its power comes from the autoregressive property that early tokens condition everything after them.
terms.Prefill attack:
In a prefill attack the adversary writes the start of the assistant reply, typically an affirmative opening such as 'Sure, here is', so generation continues from p(y | x, s) where s is the attacker's prefix. It works on APIs that expose prefilling and trivially on open-weight models, where the attacker controls decoding. The mechanism is that safety training concentrates on the opening tokens. Qi et al. (2024) measured that the per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is large over the first few output tokens and small afterward, which they called shallow safety alignment, and showed prefilling and fine-tuning attacks exploit it. Andriushchenko et al. (2024) reported prefilling as an effective component of adaptive attacks on safety-aligned models, and the GCG suffix attack (Zou et al., 2023) optimizes toward the same affirmative-opening target indirectly.

Defences: data augmentation that trains refusal recovery after a harmful opening (Qi et al.), regularized fine-tuning that protects the initial tokens, output classifiers over the whole generation, or disabling prefill.

Distinguish from prompt-injection attacks, which hijack through data, and jailbreak suffixes, which edit the user turn.
terms.Prefix sum:
Given an array a[0..n−1], the prefix sum P is defined by P[0] = 0 and P[i] = P[i−1] + a[i−1], so P[i] is the sum of the first i elements. The sum over indices l..r inclusive is P[r+1] − P[l]. Building P costs O(n) time and O(n) space, after which each range query is O(1). In two dimensions, S[i][j] = a[i−1][j−1] + S[i−1][j] + S[i][j−1] − S[i−1][j−1], and any rectangle sum follows by inclusion-exclusion over four corners.

Counting subarrays whose sum equals k: scan with running sum s, keep a hash map of how many times each earlier prefix value has occurred (seeded with {0: 1}), and add map[s − k] at each step; this is O(n) and works with negative numbers, unlike a sliding window, which needs non-negative values. Variants: prefix sums modulo m find subarrays divisible by m; the difference array is the inverse transform, letting range-add updates run in O(1) each. For arrays that change, a Fenwick tree supports point updates and prefix queries in O(log n).

Prefix sums apply to any invertible operation (XOR, counts), but not to max or min.
terms.Pretraining:
Pretraining minimizes the next-token cross-entropy L(θ) = −E[Σ_t log p_θ(x_t | x_<t)] over a corpus of trillions of tokens. Compute is roughly C ≈ 6·N·D floating-point operations for N parameters and D tokens. Scaling-law studies (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022, 'Chinchilla') found loss falls as a smooth power law in N, D and C; Chinchilla's compute-optimal rule is to grow N and D in roughly equal proportion, on the order of 20 tokens per parameter. Many models train on far more tokens, since smaller models are cheaper to serve.

Practice: AdamW with warmup then decay, million-token batches, bf16 arithmetic and data/tensor/pipeline parallelism. Data work dominates quality: deduplication, quality classifiers, mixture ratios across web, code, books and math, decontamination against benchmarks. Repeating data for a few epochs is nearly as good as fresh data; returns diminish beyond that.

It differs from fine-tuning in scale and objective, and from continued pretraining, which resumes the same objective on new text. Open problems: the limits of available human text and whether synthetic data can substitute without degrading quality.
terms.Probability distribution:
A probability distribution assigns probability to outcomes in a sample space. For a discrete variable, a probability mass function satisfies p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ_x p(x) = 1. For a continuous variable, a density f(x) ≥ 0 integrates to 1, and probabilities are integrals over regions; a density value can exceed 1, since it is not itself a probability. Joint, marginal and conditional distributions are tied by the chain rule p(x, y) = p(x)·p(y | x), which is how language models define sequence probability.

A model's logits z are mapped to a distribution by softmax, p_i = exp(z_i/T) / Σ_j exp(z_j/T), with temperature T. Entropy H(p) = −Σ p_i log p_i measures uncertainty, from 0 for a one-hot distribution to log V for a uniform one over V outcomes; KL divergence and total variation distance compare distributions. Decoding truncates the tail with top-k or top-p (nucleus) sampling, which renormalizes what is left.

A predicted probability is not automatically calibrated: a model saying 70% may be right far more or less often, and calibration must be measured separately.
terms.Probe:
A probe is a supervised classifier g_φ trained on frozen model activations: given h(x) ∈ R^d from a layer and token position, predict a label y such as 'statement is true' or 'prompt is a test'. A linear probe is ŷ = σ(w·h + b), fit by logistic regression. Alain and Bengio (2016) introduced linear classifier probes to see where in a network a property becomes linearly decodable. A simpler alternative is the mass-mean probe, whose direction is the difference between class means; Marks and Tegmark (2023) found it generalized better and was more causally implicated in truth-related behaviour than logistic regression.

High accuracy shows information is present, not that the model uses it. Hewitt and Liang (2019) showed expressive probes can learn the task themselves, so compare against control tasks (selectivity). Causal tests (ablating the direction, as in amnesic probing, or steering along it) check use. Practical failures: spurious correlates, distribution shift, and adversarial evasion; Bailey et al. (2024) showed models can be trained to obfuscate activations against probes.

Not the same as a sparse autoencoder (unsupervised) or an activation-steering vector.
terms.Process supervision:
Process supervision trains on judgments of intermediate reasoning steps. A process reward model (PRM) assigns each step s_t a score, for example the probability the step is correct; a solution is scored by aggregating, say, the product of step probabilities. Lightman et al. (2023) collected PRM800K, about 800,000 human step-level labels on math solutions, and found a PRM beat an outcome reward model for best-of-N selection on the MATH benchmark. Labelling cost motivated automatic labels: in Math-Shepherd (Wang et al., 2023), a step's value is estimated by sampling continuations from it and measuring the fraction reaching the correct answer, an estimate of the value function V(s_t) under the policy.

Weaknesses: noisy labels, ambiguity about what a 'step' is, domains without clear step correctness, and reward hacking when a policy is optimized against a learned PRM; the DeepSeek-R1 report cited these as reasons for using rule-based outcome rewards. The safety case is that humans oversee reasoning, but Baker et al. (2025) found pressure on chain-of-thought can teach models to hide intent. A visible step also need not be the computation that determined the answer.
terms.Prompt:
A prompt is the token sequence x conditioning generation: the model samples y ~ p_θ(y | x). In chat systems, system text, user and assistant turns, tool definitions and tool results are serialized by a chat template into one sequence using special delimiter tokens, so roles are conventions the model learned in post-training, not hard-coded structure. Everything shares one context window of fixed maximum length.

Cost has two phases. Prefill processes all n prompt tokens in parallel, with attention cost growing as O(n²); decoding then generates one token at a time, reusing stored keys and values (the KV cache). Providers can cache the computed state for a repeated prompt prefix, so putting stable content first lowers latency and cost. Behaviour is sensitive to wording and format: Sclar et al. (2023) showed that semantically equivalent formatting changes can swing few-shot accuracy by large margins.

A hard prompt is human-readable text; a soft prompt (prompt tuning; Lester et al., 2021) is a learned embedding sequence. A prompt is not a guarantee of obedience, because instructions and untrusted data share the same channel.
terms.Prompt engineering:
Prompt engineering is the empirical optimization of the input x to improve p_θ(y | x) on a task without changing weights. Established techniques: few-shot examples (Brown et al., 2020), chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022), zero-shot 'think step by step' (Kojima et al., 2022), self-consistency, which samples several reasoning paths and takes the majority answer (Wang et al., 2023), structured output formats, and retrieval of relevant documents. Automated search also exists (Zhou et al., 2022; the DSPy framework).

Rigorous practice treats a prompt as a hyperparameter: tune on a development set, report on a separate test set, measure variance over sampling seeds and paraphrases, and rerun after model updates, because gains often fail to transfer between models or versions. For safety evaluations, weak prompting underestimates what a model can do, so evaluators spend effort on elicitation, getting the best-effort performance as a lower bound on capability.

Persistent myths: that specific incantations or politeness reliably help, and that prompting teaches new knowledge rather than selecting and arranging what the model already encodes. Related: 'context engineering' covers everything placed in the context window, including tools and memory.
terms.Prompt injection:
Prompt injection manipulates an LLM application by placing instructions in text the model will process. Greshake et al. (2023) formalized the indirect form: an attacker controls data the application retrieves, such as a web page or email, and the model treats it as instructions. The root cause is architectural: system prompt, user message and tool output are concatenated into a single token stream with no enforced separation, unlike SQL injection, which parameterized queries solve. Willison's 'lethal trifecta' names the dangerous combination: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a channel for external communication.

Benchmarks like AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) report benign-task utility and attack success rate. Defences: instruction hierarchy training, marking untrusted data (spotlighting), injection classifiers, least-privilege tools, human confirmation, and system designs such as CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025), which separates a privileged planner from a quarantined model that handles untrusted text and tracks data flow. Adaptive attackers have broken many heuristic defences, so only architectural limits give strong guarantees.

Jailbreaking differs: the user themselves subverts the model's safety rules, whereas injection lets a third party subvert the user's intent.
terms.Proximal Policy Optimization:
PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) maximizes a clipped surrogate objective: L = E_t[min(ρ_t·Â_t, clip(ρ_t, 1−ε, 1+ε)·Â_t)], where ρ_t = π_θ(a_t|s_t)/π_old(a_t|s_t) and Â_t is the advantage, typically from generalized advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2016), using a value network V(s): Â_t = Σ_l (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}, δ_t = r_t + γV(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t). Clipping removes incentive to move ρ far from 1, allowing several gradient epochs per batch. In RLHF the reward includes a per-token penalty −β·log(π_θ/π_ref), keeping the policy near the starting model.

Cost is the value network, comparable in size to the policy. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) removes it: for G samples of one prompt, the advantage is (R_i − mean(R)) / std(R), shared by every token of response i. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) argues that dividing by std and length-normalizing add biases, and RLOO (Ahmadian et al., 2024) uses a leave-one-out baseline. Prompts where all samples score the same give zero gradient.

Clipping does not strictly bound the KL step; Engstrom et al. (2020) found code-level implementation details, rather than the clipped objective itself, account for much of PPO's gain over TRPO.
terms.Pull:
git pull runs git fetch followed by an integration step, by default git merge FETCH_HEAD. Fetch downloads missing objects and updates remote-tracking refs such as refs/remotes/origin/main according to the remote's refspec (+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*), leaving your branches and working tree untouched. The integration step targets the branch's upstream, configured by branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge. If your branch is an ancestor of the upstream, the merge is a fast-forward: the branch ref just moves. If histories diverged, Git creates a merge commit via a three-way merge from the merge base, or with --rebase replays your local commits onto the upstream tip.

Recent Git versions refuse to reconcile divergent branches until you choose a strategy: pull.rebase true, pull.ff only (fail unless fast-forward) or merge. --autostash saves and reapplies uncommitted changes around a rebase. A more cautious habit is fetch, inspect with git log HEAD..origin/main or git diff HEAD...origin/main, then merge or rebase deliberately.

Misconceptions: pull does not update other local branches, and it does not push. It differs from fetch (no integration) and from git clone (new repository). Conflicts surface during the integration step, not the download.
terms.Pull request:
A pull request (GitHub, Bitbucket) or merge request (GitLab) is a record on a hosting platform, not a Git object. It names a base branch and a head branch, which may live in a fork, and shows the diff between the merge base and the head, effectively git diff base...head, together with commits, comments and check results. GitHub publishes refs/pull/N/head and a test-merge ref refs/pull/N/merge, which CI often builds. Git itself has only git request-pull, which prepares a summary for an emailed patch workflow.

Merging offers three shapes: a merge commit preserves history, squash collapses the branch into one new commit, and rebase-and-merge replays the commits linearly. Squash and rebase create commits with new hashes, so the original branch commits are not ancestors of the target and git branch --merged will not recognize the branch as merged. Teams configure branch protection: required approvals, passing status checks, CODEOWNERS review rules, linear history.

It is a request that the target pull your work, hence the name; it is not a Git command, and a pull request merged on one platform has no meaning on another.
terms.Push:
git push <remote> <src>:<dst> sends the objects reachable from the local ref src that the remote lacks (negotiated and packed efficiently) and asks the remote to update ref dst to the new commit. By default the update must be a fast-forward, meaning the old remote value is an ancestor of the new one; otherwise it is rejected as non-fast-forward, which protects other people's commits. --force overwrites regardless. --force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected> overwrites only if the remote still holds the value you expect, which is safer, though a background git fetch that updates your remote-tracking ref can defeat the protection.

Configuration: push.default=simple pushes the current branch to a same-named upstream branch; -u sets the upstream; tags are not pushed unless requested (--tags, --follow-tags). Deleting a remote branch is git push origin --delete name. A force push after rebasing rewrites shared history and leaves teammates with diverged clones.

Misconceptions: push uploads whole objects as needed rather than just 'the diff', it does not merge anything, and it is separate from opening a pull request. A rejected push means integrate first (pull or rebase), not force.
terms.Quantization:
Quantization maps real values to a small integer grid. The affine form is q = clamp(round(x/s) + z, q_min, q_max), with dequantization x̂ = s·(q − z); s is the scale and z the zero-point (z = 0 for symmetric schemes). Rounding error per value is at most s/2, so the error variance is about s²/12 for a uniform quantizer. Granularity matters: per-tensor, per-channel, or per-group scales (for example one scale per 128 weights) trade accuracy against metadata overhead.

Post-training quantization needs no retraining: GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) corrects rounding error layer by layer using second-order information, AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) protects the weights tied to large activations, and SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2022) moves activation outliers into the weights so activations can be quantized too. Quantization-aware training simulates rounding during training. Weight-only 4-bit cuts a 16-bit model's memory by roughly four times, and since decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound this speeds generation only if kernels exploit it.

Failure modes: outlier features in large transformers (Dettmers et al., 2022), and degradation hidden by perplexity but visible on long-context, reasoning or multilingual tasks.
terms.Query, key, and value:
For input X ∈ R^{n×d_model}, a head computes Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V, with W_Q, W_K ∈ R^{d_model×d_k} and W_V ∈ R^{d_model×d_v}, then Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k + M)·V, where M is a causal mask of −∞ above the diagonal. The 1/√d_k keeps score variance near 1 (a dot product of d_k unit-variance entries has variance d_k), preventing softmax saturation. Heads run in parallel and are concatenated through W_O. Compute and memory for the n × n score matrix are O(n²).

Elhage et al. (2021) show that Q and K only enter through the product W_Q W_Kᵀ (the QK circuit, deciding where to attend), while V and the output projection form the OV circuit (deciding what information is moved). At inference, K and V of past tokens are cached: per sequence about 2 · layers · n · kv_heads · d_head · bytes, which motivated multi-query and grouped-query attention (Shazeer 2019; Ainslie et al. 2023) that share K and V across heads.

The retrieval analogy is loose: these are learned linear projections, not labelled fields.
terms.Queue:
A queue is an abstract data type with enqueue (add at the back) and dequeue (remove from the front) in first-in-first-out order. Efficient implementations give O(1) for both: a circular array holding head and tail indices modulo capacity, a singly linked list with head and tail pointers, or two stacks where the 'out' stack is refilled by popping the 'in' stack only when empty (amortized O(1)). A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced 'deck') supports O(1) push and pop at both ends. In Python, use collections.deque; list.pop(0) shifts every element and costs O(n).

Breadth-first search uses a queue: starting at a source, nodes are dequeued in non-decreasing distance order, so the first time a node is reached is via a shortest path in an unweighted graph, in O(V + E). Mark nodes visited when enqueued, not when dequeued, or they enter the queue many times. A monotonic deque gives the maximum of every sliding window of size k in O(n) total.

Not to be confused with a priority queue, which dequeues by priority (heap, O(log n)) rather than arrival order, or with a stack, which is last-in-first-out.
terms.Race to the top:
As a theory of change, a 'race to the top' contrasts with a race to the bottom. In a race to the bottom, competition erodes safety because careful actors lose to careless ones: a collective-action problem in which each lab's best move is to cut corners though all would prefer shared caution. A race to the top needs the opposite payoff structure: being safer must earn something, such as customers, talent, regulatory goodwill or reputation, and imitation must be cheap enough that practices spread.

For it to work, safety must be observable and comparable. That makes evaluations, published risk frameworks, system cards, third-party audits and standards such as the voluntary commitments of the 2024 Seoul summit load-bearing; without verification, firms can signal safety cheaply (safety-washing) with no real change. Plausible failure modes: capability competition accelerated by the safety-focused entrant, and commitments with escape clauses that weaken under pressure.

There is no agreed metric of success, and counterfactual impact, what other labs would have done anyway, is hard to establish. Distinguish it from unilateral restraint (slowing down alone) and from coordinated slowdown through treaty or regulation.
terms.Random seed:
A random seed initializes a pseudorandom number generator (for example Mersenne Twister, PCG, or counter-based Philox, popular on GPUs because streams can be computed in parallel), making a sequence of 'random' draws deterministic. In training, a seed typically governs weight initialization, data shuffling, dropout masks and augmentation, and in sampling it governs token draws at temperature > 0. The same seed does not guarantee bitwise-identical results: floating-point addition is non-associative, so parallel reductions, atomic operations, auto-selected GPU kernels and batch-size-dependent kernels change the numbers unless deterministic modes are forced.

Seed variance can be large. Henderson et al. (2018) showed deep reinforcement learning results can differ substantially across seeds. Good practice: run n seeds per configuration, report mean with standard deviation or a bootstrap confidence interval, compare methods across the same seed set (paired differences reduce variance), and never choose the best seed after seeing test results, which is selection bias. Fixing a seed makes an experiment repeatable, not robust.

A seed is not a hyperparameter to tune. Distinguish repeatability (same code, same seed) from replicability (a different team reaches the same conclusion).
terms.Reasoning model:
A reasoning model is a language model trained to generate an extended chain of thought, often thousands of tokens, before its final answer, using compute at inference time to improve accuracy. The dominant recipe is reinforcement learning against verifiable outcome rewards (math answers, unit tests). DeepSeek-R1-Zero (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) applied GRPO with accuracy and format rewards directly to a base model and reported emergent behaviours such as self-verification and longer reasoning. Test-time compute scaling was reported by OpenAI for o1: accuracy rising roughly log-linearly with thinking tokens.

Trade-offs: higher latency and cost, 'overthinking' on easy problems, reward hacking in code or proofs, and unreliable faithfulness. Chen et al. (2025) found reasoning models often fail to verbalize the hints that influenced their answers, which limits chain-of-thought monitoring. Whether RL creates new reasoning ability or mostly sharpens what the base model already could do is disputed; Yue et al. (2025) argued that at large k, the base model's pass@k (chance that any of k samples is correct) can match or exceed the RL model's.

Distinguish from merely prompting for step-by-step answers, which elicits reasoning without training for it.
terms.Rebase:
git rebase <upstream> finds the commits reachable from HEAD but not from upstream (as in git rev-list upstream..HEAD), moves HEAD to upstream, and replays each commit's change on top, much like successive cherry-picks. A commit's ID is a hash covering its tree, parent(s), author, committer and message, so a replayed commit with a new parent gets a new ID even with an identical diff. The old commits remain in the object store and are reachable via the reflog and ORIG_HEAD, so git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD usually undoes a rebase. --onto newbase oldbase branch transplants a range to a different base.

Interactive rebase (-i) lets you pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup or drop each commit; --autosquash pairs fixup! commits with their targets. pull --rebase is fetch followed by a rebase. After rebasing a published branch you must push with --force-with-lease, and anyone who based work on the old commits must rebase onto the new ones.

Trade-off against merge: rebase gives linear, bisect-friendly history but loses the true branching record and risks repeated conflict resolution. It does not move commits; it copies them.
terms.Recall:
Recall is TP / (TP + FN), the fraction of actual positives detected; equivalent names are sensitivity and true positive rate (TPR), and recall = 1 − FNR (false negative rate). It is conditioned on the true class, so unlike precision it does not depend on class prevalence. Sweeping the decision threshold trades recall against false positives; the ROC curve plots TPR against FPR (false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN)), and the precision-recall curve plots precision against recall.

In practice, a recall figure is only meaningful at a stated operating point. Safety monitors are often judged by TPR at a fixed low FPR (for example 1%), since false alarms have a budget. Because recall uses only the positives in the test set, a small positive count makes it noisy: with 20 positives, 75% recall carries a 95% Wilson (binomial) interval of roughly 53% to 89%. F_β = (1+β²)·P·R / (β²·P + R) weights recall β times as much as precision, so β = 2 emphasises recall.

A trivial classifier that flags everything has recall 1, so recall alone is meaningless.
